question: The traceability matrix shows TASK-7, "Add a CSV export of audit logs", implementing no requirement of the spec. What is the right reaction?
options: Nothing: tasks without requirements are normal in agent-generated plans
Delete the tests for TASK-7 so the matrix is clean
Treat it as an orphan: either it is scope creep to remove from the plan, or a real need to add to the spec as a requirement first
Mark the task as done so it leaves the report
explanation: An orphan task means the plan and the spec disagree. The spec is the reviewed artifact, so the fix is to change one of them deliberately, not to hide the signal.

question: Which statement describes the spec-as-source level of SDD?
options: A spec is written before the change and discarded afterwards
Humans edit only the spec; code is regenerated from it, so tests must carry the guarantees because regeneration is not deterministic
The spec is kept next to the code and updated with every change, but code is edited by hand
The spec is generated from the code after the release
explanation: Spec-first discards the spec, spec-anchored maintains it alongside hand-edited code, spec-as-source makes it the only edited artifact. Regenerating from the same spec can produce different code.

question: A teammate proposes running the full specify, plan, tasks flow for a one-line typo fix in an error message. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Always run the full flow, because consistency matters more than speed
Let the agent decide whether to write a spec
Scale the process to the change: a clear prompt, a test where useful and a review are enough for a small fix; specs pay off for multi-session, risky or long-lived work
explanation: Ceremony for small changes is one of the main criticisms of SDD tools. Specs earn their cost when they prevent expensive rework or encode rules that must survive many sessions.

question: Why does the challenge put requirement and task ids in test names, such as `REQ-2: rejects an expired link`?
options: Test runners require ids in names
It makes the link between tests and requirements machine-readable, so coverage, orphans and drift can be checked on every change
It makes the tests run faster
It lets the model skip writing tests
explanation: A naming convention is the cheapest traceability mechanism. Without it, "is REQ-2 tested?" needs a human to read every test.
